newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan rebels capture key town, thrust north.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rebels capture key town, thrust north.

text.p: The Afghan Taleban militia captured the strategic government-held town of Sarobi east of Kabul overnight and thrust north towards a government airbase.
Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's Hezb-i-Islami faction, which had controlled Sarobi, confirmed that the Taleban had seized the town, 70 km (44 miles) east of the Afghan capital.
"Sarobi has fallen and Hezb-i-Islami fighters blew up an ammunition dump and some vehicles as they retreated," said a Hezb-i-Islami source in the Pakistani city of Peshawar.
The Taleban seized Sarobi at about midnight (1900 GMT Tuesday) in a two-pronged assault after resistance died away, Taleban sources in Pakistan said.
They said the militia had also taken the nearby Naghlu Dam and hydro-electric plant that began supplying power to parts of Kabul only 10 days ago after a break of two and a half years.
The capture of the town was the latest in a series of spectacular Taleban gains in eastern Afghanistan this month and a big setback to President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government.
It was another blow to Hekmatyar, who has now lost virtually all the territory previously controlled by Hezb-i-Islami.

Taleban sources said the Islamic rebels were now advancing northwards from Naghlu up the Tagab Valley that leads to the main government airbase at Bagram, 50 km (31 miles) north of Kabul, backed by hundreds of fresh troops from Jalalabad.
"Sarobi has been taken over completely," a Taleban source in the northwestern Pakistani town of Peshawar said. "Now, inshallah (God willing), we will reach Kabul."
Retreating government forces left behind many dead fighters and large quantities of weapons, the Taleban source said.

The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted Taleban sources as saying the government had lost hundreds of dead in and around Sarobi, while 105 had been captured. At least 14 Taleban fighters had been killed and 25 wounded.
Taleban sources said their forces had advanced on Sarobi northwards from Hisarak district in the adjoining Nangarhar province, and westwards along the main Jalalabad-Kabul highway.
Resistance had subsided by sunset on Tuesday while mopping up operations were completed by midnight, Taleban sources said.
Kabul radio, monitored in Islamabad, said government forces had killed 100 rebels and destroyed many military vehicles in Tuesday's battle for Sarobi, but did not report Taleban gains.
On Tuesday, the government-run radio said rockets fired by the Taleban killed three civilians and wounded nine in Kabul.
Taleban sources said a government jet dropped cluster bombs near Jalalabad airport on Tuesday, but caused no damage.
The Islamic rebels have tightened their grip on eastern provinces this month as part of a drive to seize Kabul, oust Rabbani and impose a strict Islamic order across Afghanistan.
A Taleban transport plane landed at Bagram on Tuesday, but there were conflicting accounts of the incident.

Kabul radio said the Russian-made Antonov-32 plane carrying 33 Taleban and seven Pakistani military men had been hijacked by a "brave mujahid (struggler)" on a flight between the Taleban-held cities of Herat and Kandahar.
Taleban sources confirmed that the plane had landed in Bagram, but said the pilot had defected. They denied any Pakistanis had been on board the aircraft.
Pakistan also denied the report. "This is absolutely untrue. There are no Pakistani military personnel engaged in fighting anywhere in Afghanistan," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
The Afghan government has often accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban. Islamabad denies the charge.
